title: Thermalization hierarchy from irreducible degrees of freedom
authors: Pedro Fittipaldi de Castro, Wladimir A. Benalcazar
abstract: The decomposition of the Hilbert space of a quantum many-body system into the irreducible representations of its bond and commutant algebras yields a finer structure of dynamically isolated subspaces than the mere decomposition into symmetry sectors. While it has been recognized that subspaces associated with low bond-irrep dimensions $D_λ$ tend to violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), here we show that $D_λ$ controls thermalization continuously across the full spectrum of dynamical subspaces. Using SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains as a paradigmatic example, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{log} \ D_λ$ quantitatively accounts for the average eigenstate entanglement entropy within each sector, establishing a thermalization hierarchy that interpolates from exact quantum many-body scars at $D_λ=1$ to volume-law ergodic states at large $D_λ$. To make this concrete, we introduce the notion of irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF), defined as the number of independently-varying spatial coordinates parametrizing a many-body state within a given bond-algebra sector, which provides a microscopic interpretation of $D_λ$ and of the resulting thermalization hierarchy. Finally, we show that by selectively breaking symmetries while preserving chosen bond-algebra sectors, one can embed families of nonthermal eigenstates at prescribed entanglement levels into an otherwise ergodic spectrum, generalizing restricted spectrum-generating algebras from towers of individual states to entire dynamical subspaces.
summary: The paper introduces the concept of 'irreducible degrees of freedom' (IDOF) derived from analyzing the bond algebra of quantum many-body systems. This IDOF count, $D_\lambda$, quantifies the thermalization capacity of a subspace, establishing a continuous hierarchy that smoothly interpolates between non-thermal scars and fully ergodic states. It provides an algebraic method to understand how local constraints dictate global thermal behavior.
main_problem: To establish a quantitative 'thermalization hierarchy' that refines understanding of thermalization beyond simple symmetry sector decompositions in quantum many-body systems.
main_result: The thermalization capacity is controlled by the irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF), quantified by the bond algebra irrep dimension ($D_\lambda$), establishing a continuous hierarchy from scars to ergodic states.
method: Decomposition of the Hilbert space using the bond and commutant algebras, leading to an analysis based on irreducible representations ($	ext{irreps}$) and introducing the IDOF count as a diagnostic tool.
model_or_system: The study uses SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains as a paradigmatic example. The framework analyzes how dynamics are constrained by algebraic structures derived from local interactions (bond algebra).
key_observables: Average eigenstate entanglement entropy, which is quantitatively related to $\log D_\lambda$.
important_parameters: The bond irrep dimension ($D_\lambda$), which dictates the degree of thermalization; system size $L$ and total spin $S$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the algebraic decomposition provides a finer, physically relevant structure for dynamics than simple symmetry sector decompositions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the thermalization hierarchy using diagonal blocks from the bond algebra decomposition. Other figures detail Young diagrams and specific mathematical decompositions of state amplitudes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops an algebraic framework by decomposing the Hilbert space via double-commutant pairs ($	ext{ASL}$ and $	ext{Asu}(2)$). It then applies this to analyze excitations (like two-magnon states) in terms of orthogonal components corresponding to different IDOF sectors, culminating in the definition of the thermalization hierarchy.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful algebraic tool to quantify non-equilibrium dynamics, linking microscopic structure (bond algebra irreps) directly to macroscopic thermodynamic concepts like entanglement and ergodicity. It offers a systematic way to classify quantum scars within broader ergodic regimes.
